naive.answer: Explicit selection of the most relevant segments refers to an attention mechanism that uses top-k selection to reserve the most contributive components for attention while removing irrelevant information and noise [3][4]. Through this method, the model's attention is focused more concentratedly on the most important elements of the global context [2][4].

grade.rationale: Top-k selection keeps the most contributive elements.

docintel.answer: Explicit selection refers to selecting the $k$ largest attention score elements of each row through top-k selection to ensure important components are preserved while irrelevant information and noise are removed [3][5]. Specifically, the model evaluates attention scores $P$, records the positions where component values are larger than the $k$-th largest threshold value $t_i$ of each row, and assigns negative infinity to scores smaller than the top-$k$ largest scores so their normalized probabilities approximate 0 [3][5].

grade.rationale: Top-k selection keeps the most contributive elements.

ABSTRACT
Self-attention based Transformer has demonstrated the state-of-the-art performances in a number of natural language processing tasks. Self-attention is able to model long-term dependencies, but it may suffer from the extraction of irrelevant information in the context. To tackle the problem, we propose a novel model called Explicit Sparse Transformer . Explicit Sparse Transformer is able to improve the conce

1 INTRODUCTION
Understanding natural language requires the ability to pay attention to the most relevant information. For example, people tend to focus on the most relevant segments to search for the answers to their questions in mind during reading. 3.4 Training subword level translation model
While building phrase-based SMT models at the subword level, we use (a) monotonic decoding since related languages have similar word order, (b) higher order languages models (10-gram) since data sparsity is a lesser concern owing to small vocabulary size (Vilar et al., 2007), and (c) word level tuning (by post-processing the decoder output during tuning) to optimize the co

5.4 Robustness to Domain Change
Since we are concerned with low resource scenarios, a desirable property of subword units is robustness of the translation models to change of translation domain. Kunchukuttan and Bhattacharyya (2016b) have shown that OS level models are robust to domain change. Since BPE units are learnt from a specific corpus, it is not guaranteed that they would also be robust to domain changes. To

6 Why are BPE units better than others?
The improved performance of BPE units compared to word-level and morpheme-level representations is easy to explain: with a limited vocabulary they address the problem of data sparsity . But character level models also have a limited vocabulary, yet they do not improve translation performance except for very close languages. Character level models learn character mappings effect

There are two broad set of approaches that have been explored in the literature for translation between related languages that leverage lexical similarity between source and target languages.

We trained translation systems over the following basic units: character, morpheme, word, orthographic syllable and BPE unit. docintel.answer: The N-gram language models were used to generate predictions by computing the log probability for each tweet based on the trained model [1][3]. KenLM reported the log of the probability of the N-grams, where a value closer to 0 indicated a higher probability and was associated with the tweet judged to be funnier [3]. These scores were then used to solve Subtask A (comparing two tweets to predict which one is funnier) and Subtask B (ranking a set of tweets associated with one hashtag from funniest to least funny) [1].

grade.rationale: Log-probability per tweet used to compare/rank tweets.

per_question.evidence: Stance annotation. We asked crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk to annotate whether an ETS agrees with the claim, refutes it, or has no stance towards the claim. An ETS was only considered to express a stance if it explicitly referred to the claim and either expressed support for it or refuted it. In all other cases, the ETS was considered as having no stance.

naive.answer: Semantic Web technologies (SWT) offer several opportunities to improve Machine Translation (MT), primarily by addressing lexical and syntactic ambiguity [1]. By making the semantics of content explicit, SWT can empower MT systems to produce higher quality translations while remaining scalable [3]. Specifically, the disambiguated knowledge regarding real-world entities, properties, and relationships found on the Linked Data Web can be used to infer the correct meaning of ambiguous words or sentences [3]. SWT has demonstrated capabilities in the semantic disambiguation of polysemous and homonymous words through both pre-editing techniques on source text and post-editing techniques on target language outputs [4].

grade.rationale: Covers disambiguation (pre/post-editing) but not named entities, non-standard speech or translating KBs.

docintel.answer: Semantic Web technologies (SWT) offer several opportunities to improve Machine Translation (MT), primarily by addressing lexical and syntactic ambiguity [1][2]. By making the semantics of content explicit, SWT enables MT systems to provide higher quality translations while remaining scalable [2]. Specific opportunities include using the Linked Data Web to infer the correct meaning of ambiguous sentences through knowledge of real-world entities and their relationships [2]. SWT can also address the problem of Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) words and the ambiguity of named entities by gathering knowledge from various Semantic Web resources [3]. Furthermore, these technologies can be used to augment Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models with external knowledge graphs, create multilingual linguistic ontologies for morphologically rich languages, and develop RDF multilingual dictionaries to improve translation alignment [3].

grade.rationale: Covers disambiguation and named entities but not non-standard speech or translating KBs.

per_question.evidence: This work presents data and algorithms for automatically reducing bias in text. We focus on a particular kind of bias: inappropriate subjectivity (“subjective bias”). Subjective bias occurs when language that should be neutral and fair is skewed by feeling, opinion, or taste (whether consciously or unconsciously). In practice, we identify subjective bias via the method of BIBREF2: using Wikipedia's neutral point of view (NPOV) policy. This policy is a set of principles which includes “avoiding stating opinions as facts” and “preferring nonjudgemental language”.
